Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

vice noun

a fault of character

also vices, a failing, a fault (of character)

classical

Cic. de Or. 1.247: lēgibus et praemia prōposita sunt virtūtibus et supplicia vitiīs (Lewis & Short)
Hor. Ep. 1.1.41: virtūs est vitium fugere
Traupman 402

vitium, vitiī n.

noun, second declension

a vice, a fault, a failing

Any fault or defect, of a body, a building, a speech, and above all of character, the opposite of virtūs. For a slip in writing see mistake; vitiō vertere is to count something as a fault in someone (Cic. Fam. 7.6.1).

Other words

  • prāvitās, prāvitātis f. — perverseness, a twisted disposition

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 5.2.20: quae ista est prāvitās? (Lewis & Short); Traupman 402

    Literally crookedness, deformity (Cic. Tusc. 4.29); of character, wrongheadedness rather than a particular vice.

Examples

  • avāritiam omnia vitia habēre putābant

    they held that greed contained every viceGell. 11.2.2

  • ipsam verēcundiam, vitium quidem, sed amābile

    shyness itself, a fault indeed, but a lovable oneQuint. 12.5.2

  • Quod aetās vitium posuit, aetās auferet.

    what age has put there, age will take awayPubl. Q 38

See also evil, mistake, wrong, morals, president.
